questions.question: What is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
questions.explanation: SSE enables servers to push updates to clients over a single HTTP connection. It's unidirectional (server→client only) and uses text-based event streams. Ideal for live feeds, notifications, and real-time updates.

questions.question: Which use cases are ideal for SSE? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: SSE excels at server-push scenarios: feeds, tickers, notifications. Chat with typing indicators needs bidirectional communication (client sends typing status), making WebSockets more appropriate.

questions.question: What HTTP header indicates an SSE response?
questions.explanation: SSE responses use 'Content-Type: text/event-stream'. This tells the browser to keep the connection open and parse the response as an event stream rather than a complete document.

questions.question: What built-in feature does SSE provide that WebSockets lack?
questions.explanation: SSE has built-in reconnection: browser automatically reconnects on disconnect and sends 'Last-Event-ID' header so server can resume from where client left off. WebSockets require manual reconnection logic.
The 'id' field sets the last event ID. On reconnection, browser sends this ID in 'Last-Event-ID' header, allowing server to replay missed events. Essential for reliable delivery.

questions.question: What is a limitation of SSE compared to WebSockets?

options.text: SSE is unidirectional—client cannot send data over the same connection

questions.explanation: SSE is server→client only. To send data, client must use separate HTTP requests. WebSockets provide full-duplex communication on a single connection. SSE is simpler but less flexible.

questions.question: How does SSE handle connection limits in browsers?

options.text: Each SSE connection counts against the per-domain limit (~6)
SSE uses UDP to avoid limits

questions.explanation: SSE uses standard HTTP, so connections count against browser limits (~6 per domain). Multiple tabs with SSE can exhaust limits. HTTP/2 multiplexing helps by sharing one TCP connection.

questions.question: Which SSE event fields are standard? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: SSE defines four fields: 'data' (message content), 'event' (event type/name), 'id' (event identifier for resumption), 'retry' (reconnection delay in ms). All are optional except data for meaningful events.

questions.question: A stock trading platform needs to push price updates. Why might SSE be preferred over WebSockets?

options.text: SSE works through HTTP proxies and firewalls more reliably

questions.explanation: SSE uses standard HTTP, working through proxies and firewalls that might block WebSocket upgrades. For server-push only scenarios (price feeds), SSE's simplicity and compatibility are advantages.

questions.question: What happens if an SSE connection is interrupted?

options.text: Browser automatically reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID
User must manually refresh the page

questions.explanation: SSE has built-in reconnection. Browser automatically reconnects (default 3 seconds, configurable via 'retry' field) and sends 'Last-Event-ID' header so server can resume the stream.

questions.question: True or False: SSE can only send text data, not binary.
questions.explanation: SSE is text-based (UTF-8). Binary data must be encoded (Base64) before sending, adding overhead. WebSockets natively support binary frames, making them better for binary data transfer.

questions.question: An SSE implementation sends 'retry: 5000' in the event stream. What does this configure?

options.text: Reconnection delay of 5 seconds after disconnect

questions.explanation: The 'retry' field sets the reconnection delay in milliseconds. 'retry: 5000' tells the browser to wait 5 seconds before attempting to reconnect after a connection loss.
